analysis.title: Global Data Watch
key_insights: Global real consumer spending (ex-China) grew 2.7%ar through the mid-year energy shock. JPM expects 1.8%ar this quarter. Global retail volumes slowed to 0.6%ar in the three months through September.

JPM expects next week's US October personal income report to show a second consecutive month of flat real consumption, driven by the September-October rebound in energy prices squeezing purchasing power.
Better-than-expected October US retail sales and Chase card data cut the risk of a 4Q26 US spending stall. JPM raised its 4Q US consumption forecast to 2%ar.
Brent crude has reversed nearly all of its recent rise on energy supply-demand balance. Jet fuel and US gasoline prices have also fallen.
Available October activity readings (US industrial production and employment, Asia exports and orders) point to broad demand gains alongside the concentrated tech-spending boom.
JPM projects the November flash composite PMI to decline to 53.5, consistent with 4Q26 DM GDP growth modestly above its 1.7%ar forecast. Global GDP growth is forecast at 2.7%ar in 4Q26.

Next week's US GDP revisions should show a further surge in profits. JPM expects strong profits and broadening demand to lift global employment growth toward 1%ar and sustain US job gains at a triple-digit monthly pace.

JPM's 2027 concern is that financial market stress could disrupt the expansion. It argues the 'magical thinking' that inflation will subside without weak demand is ending, and expects core inflation persistence and labor market tightening to return.

Credit intermediation is the key pressure point: elevated asset prices rest on optimistic earnings expectations that increasingly depend on capital market access. JPM flags a possible negative loop between falling asset prices, earnings expectations and tighter credit availability.
Fed rhetoric has shifted hawkish sharply in recent weeks and has moved beyond the signal from other DM central banks, per JPM's NLP Hawk-Dove Score.
October FOMC minutes gave reasons for pausing, but 'almost all participants' saw further tightening ahead. Only 'a few' thought policy may need to turn 'more restrictive'.
JPM expects the December FOMC median to project rates above 4.5%, and its forecast now includes consecutive Fed moves at the three upcoming meetings.

The rapid fall in equity prices this month is likely linked to the hawkish Fed shift. JPM sees a modest near-term drag on consumers, with the closer link running through credit. The health of business credit growth is the clearest signal of a growth drag from the correction.
Euro area is JPM's greatest growth concern among DM economies, with job growth and demand indicators weaker last quarter. JPM expects next week's PMI to be stable and 4Q GDP at 1.3%ar.

ECB: core inflation is expected to hold at 2.7%ar in 1H27, keeping two more hikes on track (December, March). Reported ECB personnel changes (Hernandez de Cos as President, Brunnermeier as Chief Economist, Boone on Market Operations) point to continuity on rates and balance sheet policy.

BoE: JPM still expects the next hike in February and sees market pricing for a back-to-back December move as excessive. October inflation came in materially below the BoE's forecast, payrolls kept declining, and indirect energy effects are absent.

China growth risks tilt down again. October industrial production slowed to 4.8%oya and fixed investment contracted 16.1%oya, with housing and infrastructure weak. JPM keeps its 4.6% 2026 GDP forecast, which depends on faster execution of back-loaded bond issuance and the CNY800bn policy-bank facility.

BoJ: JPM still expects a hike next month and moved the following hike forward from April to March. A roughly quarterly pace takes the policy rate to 2.25% by end-2027. Japan's 3Q slowdown reflected temporary factors (energy imports, rain, Kumamoto earthquakes).
EM tightening is broadening. Bank Indonesia hiked 25bp this week, in line with JPM's out-of-consensus call, and JPM expects another 25bp in December. JPM expects a 25bp BoK hike next week.

SARB held at 7.25% on a 4-3 vote. JPM now expects a 25bp hike in January and sees a 40% probability of another in March if FX pressure intensifies. JPM dropped its BoI cut call and still expects a 25bp NBH cut in December.

LatAm is slowing. JPM expects Brazil 3Q GDP to contract 1%ar and cut its 2026 forecast by 0.2pt to 1.5%. Mexico is the exception, with growth of around 2% into early 2027. JPM sees El Niño subtracting about 70bp from Peru's growth next year and expects Chile to rebound.

tension_points.bull_case: Incoming activity data show the expansion on firmer footing. Strong profits and broadening demand should lift global employment growth toward 1%ar and sustain US job gains at a triple-digit monthly pace. Income gains and lower energy prices should keep consumer spending near 2%ar.
tension_points.bear_case: The 2027 immaculate disinflation hope is set to be dashed as core inflation persistence and labor market tightening re-emerge. Elevated asset prices rest on optimistic earnings expectations that depend on capital market access, which risks a negative loop between falling asset prices, earnings expectations and tighter credit.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The health of business credit growth is the clearest signal. A market adjustment that derails the current upturn in business credit would show a building growth drag.

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed's hawkish shift is gathering steam, and JPM expects consecutive moves at the three upcoming meetings.
theme_stances.evidence: Our forecast now incorporates consecutive moves at the three upcoming meetings.

theme_stances.key_argument: The closer link between equity valuations and credit channels makes business credit the clearest signal of a growth drag.
